scenes.tts: Two drafts of the human genome appeared in 2001. The first assembly with no gaps, for all but one chromosome, came in 2022. The machines got faster every year, so why the wait? Speed was never the bottleneck. No instrument reads a chromosome in one pass. Every method reads pieces, and a genome is only as good as the way the pieces are put back together.
scenes.visual: A long genome bar with a question mark; it breaks into short reads that scatter, and a jigsaw-like gap marker asks how to join them.
scenes.narration: Two drafts of the human genome appeared in 2001. The first assembly with no gaps, for all but one chromosome, came in 2022. The machines got faster every year, so why the wait? scenes.tts: First, count the pieces. A read is the sequence reported from one fragment. Coverage is how many reads, on average, lie over each base. Coverage equals reads times read length, divided by genome length. For a human genome of three point one billion bases, thirty-fold coverage with 150-base reads needs about 620 million reads.

Coverage equals reads times read length, divided by genome length. For a human genome of 3.1 billion bases, 30-fold coverage with 150-base reads needs about 620 million reads.
scenes.visual: Reads stack over a genome bar; a depth count appears; the formula builds and is filled in with the lesson's numbers.
scenes.narration: First, count the pieces. A read is the sequence reported from one fragment. Coverage is how many reads, on average, lie over each base. Coverage equals reads times read length, divided by genome length. For a human genome of 3.1 billion bases, 30-fold coverage with 150-base reads needs about 620 million reads.

scenes.tts: Reads start at random positions, so thirty-fold is a mean, not a guarantee. Under a Poisson model, the fraction of bases with no read is e to the minus C. At one-fold, thirty-seven percent is unread. At five-fold, about 21 million bases are unread. At thirty-fold, far less than one base is expected. So more depth shrinks the gaps that random sampling leaves.

scenes.visual: A plot of e to the minus C is drawn; points at C of 1 and 5 are marked with their unread amounts, then 30 is shown falling off the end.

scenes.tts: Depth cannot fix a different problem. Give the genome two identical copies of a six-kilobase repeat. A read from inside the repeat fits both copies equally well. Reads at its edges are unique. But no read, and no pair from a 400-base fragment, reaches across six kilobases to the far edge. So the assembler cannot tell which flanking sequences belong together.

scenes.visual: Two identical repeat blocks sit between four unique flanks; a short read fits both blocks; a short pair cannot reach the far edge; two possible joinings of the flanks are shown with question marks.
scenes.narration: Depth cannot fix a different problem. Give the genome two identical copies of a 6-kilobase repeat. A read from inside the repeat fits both copies equally well. Reads at its edges are unique. But no read, and no pair from a 400-base fragment, reaches across 6 kilobases to the far edge. So the assembler cannot tell which flanking sequences belong together.

scenes.tts: Deeper coverage adds more reads of the same ambiguous kind. Extra depth does not change what each read can say. Every new read from inside the repeat still fits both copies. The assembler collapses the two copies into one, or it breaks the contig.
scenes.visual: Many more short reads pile onto the repeats, each still matching both; the repeats then collapse into one block, or the contig breaks apart.
scenes.narration: Deeper coverage adds more reads of the same ambiguous kind. Extra depth does not change what each read can say. Every new read from inside the repeat still fits both copies. The assembler collapses the two copies into one, or it breaks the contig.

scenes.tts: Now try a 15-kilobase read instead of a 150-base read. It can hold a whole six-kilobase copy with several kilobases of unique sequence on each side. That pins the copy in place. Long reads span repeats that short reads cannot. Keep this rule: a repeat longer than your reads cannot be placed, and more depth does not help.
